title: Pipe Bowl

altText: A small carved pipe bowl of dark argillite stone, about six by ten centimeters, with whales as part of its design.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, date, medium, culture, country, credit line, objectName (Pipe bowl), tag (Whales), dimensions, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record. The record has no classification.

context: A small carved pipe bowl made of argillite by Haida artists in the early 19th century, dated 1815 to 1820. The record tags whales as its subject. It measures about 6.4 by 9.5 centimeters. Argillite is a fine-grained stone that Haida carvers have long worked.

descriptions.k: This little carving is made of dark stone. It shows whales. It is small enough to hold in your hand. Haida artists carved it. Can you find a whale? What shapes do you see?
descriptions.g12: Haida artists carved this small object from a dark, smooth stone called argillite. Whales are part of the carving. It is called a pipe bowl, and it is about as wide as your palm. Imagine the carver's tiny tools. What details can you find?
descriptions.g35: This pipe bowl was carved by Haida artists between 1815 and 1820 from argillite, a fine-grained stone that can be carved in detail. Whales appear in its design. The carving is only about 9.5 centimeters wide, so every detail is small. Look at how the carver fit the whales into the shape of the bowl. Why would an artist choose whales?
descriptions.g68: Haida carvers began making argillite pieces for trade in the early 19th century, and this pipe bowl from 1815 to 1820 is a fine small example. Argillite is soft enough to carve in detail yet takes a smooth polish. The record lists whales as the subject, but it does not say what story, if any, they illustrate. Looking closely at how the carver fits sculpted forms into a very small object shows both skill and design thinking.
descriptions.g910: This argillite pipe bowl, dated 1815 to 1820, shows Haida carvers working in a stone that could be shaped with great detail. Argillite objects made in this period often served as sculptures as well as functional forms, and sometimes reached a trading audience. The whales in the design challenge the carver to fit flowing forms into a compact object. Because the record does not interpret the imagery, careful description comes before claims about story or symbolism.
descriptions.g1112: A Haida argillite pipe bowl of 1815 to 1820, this object belongs to an early phase of a carving tradition in which artists adapted a local stone to new forms and new audiences. Whales, tagged in the record, appear within a compact sculptural design that rewards close looking. The object's date and size suggest both craft mastery and a particular historical moment, but the record does not explain the imagery or its meaning. Interpretation should rest on visible evidence and respect for Haida knowledge.

teacherNote.context: The Haida live on Haida Gwaii, off the coast of British Columbia, Canada, and are renowned carvers. Argillite carving is a distinct Haida tradition; the record lists whales as the subject and does not explain the imagery.
directions: Have students carve a small design in soap or soft clay and notice how detail changes with size.
Ask students to compare how a small carving and a large mural require different planning.
Discuss why the descendants of makers should have a voice in how museum objects are explained.
